subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 7 periods = 280 minutes
Total: 7 periods · 4h 40min

section_titles: Bird Watching — Directions on a Camp Map
periods.activity_title: Body as Compass, Then a Bird-Camp Map

tasks_in_class.description: Manu faces the rising Sun; fill: that direction is ___, left hand points ___ direction, right hand points ___ direction; which way is west?
Read clues about tent positions (west of road, closest to lake, north of green, south of lake); colour tents accordingly; draw a tent east of the lake.

time_bands.activity: Children stand, face the window where the Sun rises, and enact the body-compass: arms spread wide, left pointing behind and right in front are named North and South while the class agrees on labels together. The teacher reads the poem 'Four Little Chicks' aloud and children point each direction as it is named.

p.171 ("Manu faces the rising Sun; fill: that direction is ___, left hand points…") — children complete the blanks individually, then pairs compare and justify their reasoning aloud: 'My right hand points West because…'

Bird Watching!, p.172 ("Read clues about tent positions… colour tents accordingly; draw a tent east of the lake.") — the teacher reads each clue aloud; small groups decode the relative position, shade tents on their maps, and draw the new east-of-lake tent. Groups share their east-tent placement and explain the direction used.

periods.teacher_notes: Children often confuse left-right with North-South when they turn their bodies; anchor the correction by returning to 'face the rising Sun first, then your left is always North.' The conceptual shift from body-anchored direction to map-top-down direction in the Bird Watching activity is deliberate — allow time for the group discussion so children surface and resolve this shift themselves. Watch for children who colour a tent 'closest to the lake' without also checking the other clues; prompt them to re-read all clues before colouring.

periods.activity_title: Reading a Room Map, Then Drawing Your Own

tasks_in_class.description: Write the directions of window, bed, cupboard, and bedside table in relation to the girl in the room diagram.
Make a drawing of your room; locate directions of things from the centre; draw the direction arrow for your room.
Write the names of things placed in East, West, North, and South directions in your room.

time_bands.activity: Map of a Room, p.172 ("Write the directions of window, bed, cupboard, and bedside table in relation to the girl…") — children study the room diagram, stand to mimic the girl's facing direction, then write each object's direction. Pairs compare answers and correct mismatches.

Map of a Room, p.173 ("Make a drawing of your room; locate directions of things from the centre; draw the direction arrow for your room.") — children sketch a freehand plan of their own room, mark the centre, and draw a compass arrow. An unhurried making activity: the teacher circulates and asks 'Which wall faces North in your room?'

Map of a Room, p.173 ("Write the names of things placed in East, West, North, and South directions in your room.") — children use their own sketch to list objects in each cardinal direction. A quick count round the class collects one East object from each child to check variety and accuracy.

periods.teacher_notes: Children sometimes write a direction relative to themselves sitting at a desk rather than relative to the figure in the diagram; model 'stand where the girl stands, face where she faces' before they write. When children draw their own rooms, some may not know which wall faces North — suggest they recall where the Sun enters in the morning as an anchor. The progression from reading someone else's map to drawing and annotating their own room is the key conceptual step in this section.

section_titles: Zoo Trip — Street Map and Bus Route
periods.activity_title: Navigating the Bus Route on a Street Map

tasks_in_class.description: Fill blanks: bus goes north from parking, turns right onto ___ Road driving ___ direction to reach S1; turns right/left onto ___ Road driving ___ direction to reach S2.
(a) Houses east of Jaideep's; (b) route from Ravi's house to children's park; (c) stop closer to Lali's house; (d) route for Golu to nearest stop; (e) direction for Prem to reach Stop 2.

time_bands.activity: The teacher displays or directs children to the street map on p.174. Together the class identifies the compass rose, names the three roads, and locates the two bus stops. Children trace the bus route with a finger before reading any questions.

Bus Route, p.174 ("Fill blanks: bus goes north from parking, turns right onto ___ Road driving ___ direction to reach S1…") — children trace the route aloud step by step, filling each blank. The teacher pauses after 'turns right' to ask 'If you are driving north and turn right, which direction are you now facing?' so reasoning is made explicit.

Bus Route, p.174 ("(a) Houses east of Jaideep's; (b) route from Ravi's house to children's park; (c) stop closer to Lali's house; (d) route for Golu to nearest stop; (e) direction for Prem to reach Stop 2.") — small groups tackle one sub-question each, then the class assembles the full set of answers with each group presenting their reasoning.

periods.teacher_notes: A common error is treating 'turn right' as always meaning East — children must re-orient relative to their current direction of travel. Prompt with 'Which direction are you going before you turn?' as they work through the route blanks. The multi-part Bus Route task is the chapter's most complex directional reasoning task; distributing sub-questions across groups ensures every child contributes to at least one part.

periods.activity_title: Reading the Metro Map — Legend, Lines, and Routes

tasks_in_class.description: Read the key; identify symbols on the metro map; name what different coloured lines represent; mark Qutb Minar on Yellow Line and Supreme Court on Blue Line.
(a) Trace different routes Qutb Minar→Supreme Court; (b) Lali's suggestion — which stations to change line again; (c) route with least stations; (d) best route to zoo from Qutb Minar.

homework.description: Make a map of school with key for symbols; hide objects; mark positions with red dots/flags; challenge friends to find hidden things using the map.

time_bands.activity: Delhi Metro Train Stations, p.175 ("Read the key; identify symbols on the metro map; name what different coloured lines represent; mark Qutb Minar on Yellow Line and Supreme Court on Blue Line.") — children examine the colour-coded key in pairs, name each line, then individually mark the two stations on their map. The teacher asks 'How do you know a circle on the map is a station?'

Delhi Metro Train Stations, p.176 ("(a) Trace different routes Qutb Minar→Supreme Court; (b) Lali's suggestion…; (c) route with least stations; (d) best route to zoo from Qutb Minar.") — groups trace at least two different routes for (a), then work through (b)–(d) comparing interchange counts and station counts. Each group shares its 'best route' answer with one sentence of justification.

Brief class discussion: 'Can two groups have different best routes and both be right?' Children surface the idea that 'best' depends on the criterion chosen — fewest stations or fewest interchanges. The homework task Let Us Do, p.176, is introduced: children will make a map of school with a key and mark hidden objects.

periods.teacher_notes: Children sometimes assume the map legend is decoration; open with 'What would happen if you could not read the key?' to establish that decoding the legend is the first act of map reading. Watch for children who trace routes that skip interchange stations — remind them a change of line requires physically changing platforms at that station. The homework map-making task is self-contained and requires only paper, pencil, and a small object to hide.
materials: Coloured pencils (to trace routes in different colours)

section_titles: Anthill in the Zoo — Grid Distances and Directions
periods.activity_title: Ant Trails: Direction and Distance on a Grid

tasks_in_class.description: Fill blanks: distance and direction for ant to reach sugar (b), bread (c — two segments), apple (d — three segments); identify other routes to apple and which is shortest.

time_bands.activity: The teacher draws a simple 4×4 grid on the board with N-S-E-W arrows and marks a starting point and one food item. The class is asked: 'How would you tell an ant exactly how to walk from here to there?' Children suggest descriptions; the teacher models 'crawl 2 cm east then 1 cm north' to introduce direction-distance language.

Anthill in the Zoo, p.177 ("Fill blanks: distance and direction for ant to reach sugar (b), bread (c — two segments), apple (d — three segments); identify other routes to apple and which is shortest.") — children work the single-direction path to sugar first, then the two-segment path to bread, then the three-segment path to apple. Pairs compare segment descriptions and resolve differences by measuring on the grid.

Groups share alternative routes to the apple they discovered, list them on the board as direction-distance strings, and vote on which is shortest. The teacher asks 'How did you decide it was shortest — did you add the distances?' consolidating the idea of total path length.

periods.teacher_notes: Children often write direction without distance or distance without direction; insist on the paired form '2 cm East' throughout. The three-segment apple path has more than one valid solution — celebrate different valid paths and use the comparison to motivate the shortest-path question. Children who have practised naming cardinal directions from the room map and street map activities will find the grid language a natural next step.

periods.activity_title: Zoo Coordinates: East First, Then North

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Locating the Animals in the Zoological Park (Zoo), p.178
tasks_in_class.description: Fill blanks to reach tortoise: steps east→column, steps north→row; state location of tortoise (4,1); identify what is at (1,4).

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Locating the Animals in the Zoological Park (Zoo) Q1, p.178
tasks_in_class.description: Locate the animal at positions (11,11), (2,6), (6,4), (3,10), (11,3), (10,9) on the zoo grid map.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Locating the Animals in the Zoological Park (Zoo) Q2, p.178
tasks_in_class.description: Write the ordered-pair position of Lion, Elephant, Tortoise, Deer, Panda, and Crocodile on the zoo map.

homework.book_ref: Locating the Animals in the Zoological Park (Zoo) Q3, p.178
homework.description: Place coloured dots at positions (8,3) Red, (2,9) Green, (7,3) Blue, (3,8) Orange, (8,6) Black, (6,6) Pink on the zoo grid.

time_bands.activity: Locating the Animals in the Zoological Park (Zoo), p.178 ("Fill blanks to reach tortoise: steps east→column, steps north→row; state location of tortoise (4,1); identify what is at (1,4).") — the teacher walks the class through the rule 'move east first to the column number, then move north to the row number' using a finger-trace on the board grid. Children fill the blanks and then identify (1,4) independently.

Locating the Animals in the Zoological Park (Zoo) Q1, p.178 ("Locate the animal at positions (11,11), (2,6), (6,4), (3,10), (11,3), (10,9) on the zoo grid map.") — children practise moving East then North for each ordered pair, circling the animal at each intersection. A quick check: the teacher calls a coordinate and children hold up the animal name on a slip of paper.

Locating the Animals in the Zoological Park (Zoo) Q2, p.178 ("Write the ordered-pair position of Lion, Elephant, Tortoise, Deer, Panda, and Crocodile on the zoo map.") — children reverse the process, tracing from a named animal to count East then North and write the pair. Pairs swap books to check each other's ordered pairs. The homework task Q3 is introduced: children will place coloured dots at six given coordinates on the zoo grid.

periods.teacher_notes: The most common error at this stage is reversing the pair — children write (row, column) instead of (column, row); consistently ask 'Which direction do you move first?' before they write. T-12 is the concept-builder that distinguishes (4,1) from (1,4); ensure every child resolves this contrast before moving to Q1. Q3 is assigned as homework since it is procedurally similar to Q1 and children can work it independently once the rule is secure.

periods.activity_title: Consolidating Coordinates — Extended Practice and Reflection

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Locating the Animals in the Zoological Park (Zoo) Q3, p.178
tasks_in_class.description: Place coloured dots at positions (8,3) Red, (2,9) Green, (7,3) Blue, (3,8) Orange, (8,6) Black, (6,6) Pink on the zoo grid.

time_bands.activity: The class opens the zoo grid. Children who completed Q3 at home share their placements; children who did not yet have it complete it now. The teacher asks volunteers to call out a coordinate and the class finger-traces to verify the dot position together.

The teacher poses three fresh grid challenges on the board using the same 12×12 zoo grid: 'Which animal is at (6,6)?', 'Write the coordinate of an animal you choose', and 'If an animal moved 2 steps East and 3 steps North from (4,1), what is its new coordinate?' Children work individually, then pairs compare and justify their answers using the rule.

Class debrief: the teacher draws a simple 5-column table on the board labelled with the chapter's five map types — Body Compass, Camp Map, Room Map, Street Map, Metro Map, Grid Path, Coordinate Grid — and asks children to call out one thing they can now do on each kind of map that they could not do before. This surfaces the chapter's conceptual ladder without the teacher naming it explicitly.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit builds on the coordinate rule — east first, then north — that children worked with in the ordered-pairs introduction, so the fresh challenges should feel like confident application rather than new learning. Watch for children who still reverse the pair; the 'moved 2 East then 3 North' question is a good diagnostic because it requires applying the rule to a new starting point. The debrief table activity is teacher-led but child-voiced — the teacher records what children say, not a prepared list.

items.prompt: On a metro map, a key shows: Red line, Blue line, Yellow line, and circles for stations. Priya wants to travel on the Yellow Line. Which symbol should she follow?

options.label: A
options.text: A blue-coloured line on the map

options.label: B
options.text: A circle marked on the map

options.label: C
options.text: A red-coloured line on the map

options.label: D
options.text: A yellow-coloured line on the map

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A yellow-coloured line on the map.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Match the colour named in the question to the same colour in the map key.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has confused Red Line with Yellow Line, showing they have not matched the specific colour named.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student has confused the station symbol (circle) with the line symbol, showing they have not decoded what the two different symbols represent.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has confused Blue Line with Yellow Line, showing imprecise use of the colour key.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student point to each colour in the key before answering; stretch: ask the student to name what a circle symbol in the key represents.

exercise.description: Read the key; identify symbols on the metro map; name what different coloured lines represent; mark Qutb Minar on Yellow Line and Supreme Court on Blue Line.

items.prompt: Rani stands facing the rising Sun with her arms stretched out. She says her right hand points West. Is she correct? Write one sentence explaining your answer.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: No, she is not correct. When facing the rising Sun (East), the right hand points West is wrong — the right hand points South and the left hand points North.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Face East (rising Sun), then left hand is North, right hand is South, and behind is West.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student stand, face a window where the Sun rises, and spread arms before writing; stretch: ask what direction is behind Rani and why.

exercise.description: Manu faces the rising Sun; fill: that direction is ___, left hand points ___ direction, right hand points ___ direction; which way is west?

items.section_title: Bird Watching — Directions on a Camp Map
items.prompt: On a camp map, a lake is in the centre. A clue says: 'Place the blue tent south of the lake.' Where should the blue tent be drawn?

options.label: A
options.text: Above the lake on the map

options.label: B
options.text: Below the lake on the map

options.label: C
options.text: To the left of the lake on the map

options.label: D
options.text: To the right of the lake on the map

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Below the lake on the map.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: On a standard map, South is the direction shown at the bottom, so south of the lake means below it.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has confused South with North, placing the tent above (North) instead of below.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has confused South with West, showing a mix-up between vertical and horizontal directions.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has confused South with East, showing a mix-up between vertical and horizontal directions.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to point to the South arrow on the map compass rose first; stretch: ask where an East-of-the-lake tent would go.

exercise.description: Read clues about tent positions (west of road, closest to lake, north of green, south of lake); colour tents accordingly; draw a tent east of the lake.

items.prompt: Look at a room map. A girl stands in the centre of the room. The window is on the wall to her left, and her left hand points North. Write the direction of the window from the girl.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The window is to the North of the girl.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: The direction a side lies from the centre is the direction of anything on that wall; the girl's left points North, so the left wall and the window on it are North.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to spread their own arms and label left as North before answering; stretch: ask what direction the wall opposite the window (behind the girl) would be.

exercise.description: Write the directions of window, bed, cupboard, and bedside table in relation to the girl in the room diagram.

items.section_title: Zoo Trip — Street Map and Bus Route
items.prompt: A bus travels East along Park Road. It then turns left at a crossing. In which direction is the bus now travelling?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: When travelling East and turning left, the new direction is North — a left turn from East always faces North.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student thinks the bus continues East, not recognising that turning changes direction.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has applied a U-turn logic, reversing East to West instead of turning 90 degrees left.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has confused left with right — a right turn from East gives South, not a left turn.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student draw an arrow pointing East on paper, then physically turn the paper left 90 degrees to see the new direction; stretch: ask what direction a right turn from East would give.

exercise.description: (a) Houses east of Jaideep's; (b) route from Ravi's house to children's park; (c) stop closer to Lali's house; (d) route for Golu to nearest stop; (e) direction for Prem to reach Stop 2.

items.prompt: Amit travels from Station X to Station Z. Route 1 passes through 4 stations and needs 1 interchange. Route 2 passes through 6 stations and needs no interchange. Which route has fewer stations? Which route has fewer interchanges? Write both answers.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Route 1 has fewer stations (4 compared to 6). Route 2 has fewer interchanges (0 compared to 1).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare the two numbers given for each criterion separately — stations: 4 versus 6; interchanges: 1 versus 0.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: prompt the student to write the two numbers side by side for each criterion before deciding; stretch: ask the student which route they would choose and to give one reason.

exercise.description: (a) Trace different routes Qutb Minar→Supreme Court; (b) Lali's suggestion — which stations to change line again; (c) route with least stations; (d) best route to zoo from Qutb Minar.

items.section_title: Anthill in the Zoo — Grid Distances and Directions
items.prompt: An ant starts at a point on a grid. It crawls 3 cm East, then 2 cm North. Write the ant's path using direction-distance language, one segment at a time.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Segment 1: 3 cm East. Segment 2: 2 cm North.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Name the distance first, then the direction for each segment of the path in order.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to trace the path with a finger on grid paper before writing; stretch: ask the student to describe an alternative two-segment route from the same start to the same end point.

exercise.description: Fill blanks: distance and direction for ant to reach sugar (b), bread (c — two segments), apple (d — three segments); identify other routes to apple and which is shortest.

items.prompt: On a zoo grid, you move 3 steps East and then 5 steps North from the entrance. Which ordered pair names this location?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: (3, 5) — 3 steps East gives the column (first number), 5 steps North gives the row (second number).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Move East first for the first number in the pair, then move North for the second number.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has reversed the pair, writing North-steps first and East-steps second.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has used only the East distance for both numbers, ignoring the North movement.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has used only the North distance for both numbers, ignoring the East movement.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to finger-trace East first then North on the grid before writing the pair; stretch: ask what animal or object a reversed pair (5,3) would point to on the zoo grid.

exercise.book_ref: Locating the Animals in the Zoological Park (Zoo), p.178
exercise.description: Fill blanks to reach tortoise: steps east→column, steps north→row; state location of tortoise (4,1); identify what is at (1,4).

items.prompt: Imagine you are standing in the centre of a room. The door is on your North wall and the cupboard is on your East wall. Name the direction of the door and the direction of the cupboard from where you stand.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The door is to the North. The cupboard is to the East.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: The direction of an object is the cardinal direction of the wall it is on, read from the centre of the room.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: provide a worked first instance — 'The window is on the South wall, so the window is to the South'; stretch: ask the student to name what direction the wall opposite the door would be.

exercise.description: Make a drawing of your room; locate directions of things from the centre; draw the direction arrow for your room.

items.prompt: On the zoo grid, move 7 steps East and 4 steps North from the entrance. Write the ordered pair for this location.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: East steps give the first number, North steps give the second number: (7, 4).
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: remind the student to count East first and write that number before the comma; stretch: ask the student to write the ordered pair for a point that is 4 steps East and 7 steps North and explain why (4,7) and (7,4) are different locations.

exercise.book_ref: Locating the Animals in the Zoological Park (Zoo) Q1, p.178
exercise.description: Locate the animal at positions (11,11), (2,6), (6,4), (3,10), (11,3), (10,9) on the zoo grid map.

items.prompt: On a zoo grid, a Penguin is located 9 steps East and 5 steps North of the entrance. Write the ordered pair that names the Penguin's position.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count East for the first number, count North for the second number: (9, 5).
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to say aloud 'East first' before writing; stretch: ask the student to name the ordered pair for a location 5 steps East and 9 steps North and confirm it is different.

exercise.book_ref: Locating the Animals in the Zoological Park (Zoo) Q2, p.178
exercise.description: Write the ordered-pair position of Lion, Elephant, Tortoise, Deer, Panda, and Crocodile on the zoo map.
